question.problem:
Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(t)$ given that its derivative ${r}^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the corresponding unit tangent ${T}^{′}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,{T}^{′}(t)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
Since we are given both the derivative of the curve ${r}^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the unit tangent ${T}^{′}(t),$ we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Now, we find the magnitudes of ${T}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =|-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}|\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{1+1+0} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =1 \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{1+1+0} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{t}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{-t}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
